To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) multiple carrier injections are more effective than a single carrier in inducing a specific anti-cancer immune response and (ii) the sequential use of different carriers may generate more efficient anti-tumor immune response and may lead to the effective eradication of the tumor in a higher percentage than the use of a single carrier.
the use of a single carrier may be detrimental to the immune control of tumors and the use of multiple carriers, in contrast, is more efficient.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of effective cancer vaccination protocols based on the use of multiple antigens and carriers.
the development of computational models of the immune system.
the development of a computational model for the simulation of the dynamics of the adaptive immune response to tumor and of different vaccination protocols.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sequential use multiple carriers is superior to the use of single carriers for the generation of anti-cancer immune response.
the use of a single carrier may be more effective than the sequential use of two carriers.
the use of different carriers in a vaccine may be more efficient than the use of the same carrier for priming and boosting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of two or more vectors for priming and boosting may generate more effective immune responses than the use of a single one.

the use of different vectors encoding the antigen of interest may be more effective in inducing anti-tumor immune response than single carrier injections, and may represent a promising strategy in cancer vaccination.
the use of two different vectors for vaccination is more effective than the use of one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to achieve effective anti-tumor immunity, it may be necessary to prime and boost with different antigen/carrier constructs.
the use of a single vector is not always the optimal choice for cancer immunotherapy.
multiple carriers are better than a single one for the induction of anti-cancer immune response.
